question:
Patient note:
A 68-year-old man with biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis secondary to chronic genotype 1a hepatitis C infection diagnosed fifteen years earlier—successfully eradicated with a twelve-week course of ledipasvir/sofosbuvir six years ago but leaving behind portal hypertensive sequelae—was brought to the emergency department by his daughter at 08:15 because over the prior three days he had “seemed foggy,” misplaced the television remote twice, paused abnormally long when counting out change at a farm stand, and on the morning of presentation addressed his granddaughter by the wrong name before correcting himself; he also complained that his belt no longer met the usual hole by late afternoon and that turning from his back to either side in bed produced an unmistakable sloshing sensation accompanied by a sense of fullness stretching across both flanks. He denied vomiting, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, pruritus, dark urine, or recent weight loss. His prior decompensations included two outpatient large-volume paracenteses last winter and a single hospital stay three years ago for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; he had not bled from varices and had never undergone transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placement. Medications reconciled from pill bottles and a printed list were furosemide 40 mg and spironolactone 100 mg each morning—both self-discontinued two weeks earlier “because my legs were cramping”—nadolol 20 mg nightly, calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily, vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, and an over-the-counter multivitamin; he was prescribed lactulose 20 g orally twice daily after his prior admission but had taken only intermittent doses because of fear of incontinence, and he had never used rifaximin. There were no herbal supplements, anticoagulants, or psychoactive drugs in his home. He last drank alcohol—a pint of cider weekly—twelve years ago at his daughter’s insistence and has not resumed. He quit smoking two decades ago after a twenty-pack-year history. Past surgical history consisted of an open appendectomy during military service and cataract extraction in both eyes. Family history revealed a brother with hepatocellular carcinoma at 64 and a mother who died of stroke at 78; no known inherited liver disorders. He lives alone on a small farm, tends chickens, and drives short distances. Review of systems was otherwise negative for headaches, visual changes, focal weakness, urinary urgency, or rash. Pre-hospital vitals obtained by paramedics showed blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % on ambient air; no intravenous fluids or medications were given in transit. On arrival—before venipuncture, radiography, or pharmacologic therapy—temperature was 37.1 °C, blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg, heart rate 90 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 97 % breathing room air. The patient was awake, answered most questions appropriately but hesitated five seconds naming the current month, and required prompting to recall two of three objects at five minutes; handwriting on the consent form was slightly shaky, and with arms extended and wrists dorsiflexed a low-amplitude flapping tremor appeared within ten seconds. Speech was fluent without dysarthria, cranial nerves II–XII were intact, strength was 5/5 diffusely, and reflexes were physiologic. Skin inspection demonstrated scattered spider telangiectasias across the upper shoulders and a few purplish ecchymoses over the forearms; sclerae carried a subtle golden hue. Neck veins were 6 cm H₂O at 30°. Cardiac examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear. Abdominal contour was protuberant with bulging flanks that remained prominent in Fowler’s position; percussion disclosed central tympany transitioning to broad dullness over both lateral quadrants, and a pronounced fluid wave coursed from one hand to the other without the need for a third-hand stop. The umbilicus was everted but not flattened, suggesting several liters of intraperitoneal fluid; the liver edge, firm and nodular, was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, and the spleen tip was appreciable. There was mild bilateral ankle pitting to the mid-shins. Capillary glucose measured 104 mg/dL. Point-of-care ultrasound performed immediately—still prior to any therapy—revealed a shrunken heterogeneous liver with capsular nodularity, a patent portal vein with hepatopetal flow at 15 cm/s, splenomegaly measuring 16.5 cm, and anechoic free fluid accumulating to a depth of approximately 4 cm in Morrison’s pouch and layering throughout the pelvis; kidneys were normal in size and echogenicity, and no biliary dilation or focal mass was present. A bedside portable chest radiograph obtained moments later showed elevated hemidiaphragms without consolidation or pleural effusion, and a 12-lead ECG documented normal sinus rhythm at 88 beats/min with a QTc of 430 ms. Venous blood drawn through an 18-gauge antecubital catheter—documented before any intravenous albumin, diuretics, cathartics, antibiotics, vitamin K, or sedatives—returned: total bilirubin 2.37 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.58 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 55 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 78 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 162 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 210 U/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, creatinine 1.02 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.4 ×10⁹/L, platelet count 96 ×10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.68. Serum ammonia, alpha-fetoprotein, and bacterial cultures were pending at the time this note was completed. Up to this juncture the patient had received no therapeutic interventions, ensuring that all observed findings and laboratory values reflect his untreated physiologic state upon presentation for evaluation of progressive abdominal distention and new-onset cognitive slowing in the setting of advanced hepatitis C–related liver disease.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1, 2, or 3 points to each of five findings. Using pretreatment values, the ranges below are listed in 1-, 2-, 3-point order:
- Total bilirubin (<2, 2–3, >3 mg/dL): 2.37 mg/dL → 2.
- Albumin (>3.5, 2.8–3.5, <2.8 g/dL): 3.58 g/dL → 1.
- INR (<1.7, 1.7–2.3, >2.3): 1.68 is below 1.7 → 1.
- Ascites (none, slight, moderate-to-severe): bulging flanks, a pronounced fluid wave, and several liters of fluid indicate at least moderate ascites → 3.
- Hepatic encephalopathy (none, grade I–II, grade III–IV): cognitive slowing and asterixis in an awake, responsive patient support grade I–II → 2.
Total = 2 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 2 = 9 (Child-Pugh class B).
Final answer: 9
